"And the Lord spoke," it says, "unto Moses, saying: Speak unto the children of Israel, and thou shalt say unto them: Whatsoever woman shall have conceived seed and borne a male, she shall be unclean seven days." First let us consider according to the history, whether it does not seem to be added as though superfluously: "the woman who shall have conceived seed and borne a male," as if she could bear a male otherwise than by seed conceived. But it is not added superfluously. For to distinguish her who "conceived and bore" without seed, the lawgiver added this word for the sake of the other women, so that he might designate as "unclean" not every woman who had borne, but her who "had borne with seed conceived." To this may also be added that this law, which is written concerning uncleanness, pertains to women; but concerning Mary it is said that "a virgin" conceived and bore. Let the women, then, bear the burdens of the law, but let the virgins be held immune from them. […]

Now, then, let us also inquire into this: what is the cause that a woman, who furnishes a ministry to those being born into this world, is said to be made "unclean" not only when "she has received seed," but also when "she has borne"? Whence also for her purification she is commanded to offer "young pigeons or turtledoves for sin at the door of the tabernacle of testimony," that "the priest may make propitiation for her," as one who owes a propitiation and a purification of sin for the fact that she furnished a ministry to a man being born into this world. For thus it is written: "And the priest shall make propitiation for her, and she shall be cleansed." I dare say nothing in such matters, yet I perceive that certain hidden mysteries are contained in these things, and that there is something of a latent secret, on account of which even "the woman who shall have conceived of seed and borne" is called "unclean" and, as though guilty of sin, is commanded to offer a victim "for sin" and so to be purified. […]

12:3.t: Which Sabbath He in His body abolished, although, nevertheless, He had formerly Himself commanded Moses that circumcision should not pass over the eighth day, which day very frequently happens on the Sabbath, as we read written in the Gospel.
12:3.s: On the Creation of the World

12:6.t: But meanwhile she "who has borne a male," "on the eighth day" both the one who is born is circumcised and she is made clean. It is a matter of great labor for these things to happen in this brevity of time, yet, that we may say something in passing, this week may be seen as the time of the present life; for in a week of days the world was completed. In which, so long as we are set in the flesh, we cannot be pure to the point of clarity, unless the eighth day come, that is, unless the time of the age to come be present. On which day, however, he who is a male and has acted manfully is at once purified in the very coming of the age to come, and at once the mother who bore him is made clean; for she will receive the flesh purged of vices out of the resurrection. […]

13:2.t: We find, then, that six kinds are set forth concerning the leprosy of men, which six kinds are described in this manner. For either "in the skin of the body there comes a scar and a whitish sign in the skin of his body, the contagion of leprosy." Or "the leprosy flowering shall flower, and shall cover all the skin with the contagion from the head even to his feet." Or the third kind: "in the skin of the flesh there comes an ulcer and it is healed; and in the very place of the ulcer there comes a white scar." Or "in the skin of the flesh there comes a burning of fire, and" after these things "the healed burning shall be shining white, or bright with redness." The fifth kind, "when in a man or a woman there comes on the head or in the beard the contagion of leprosy." But the last kind is written, "when in baldness or in forehead-baldness there comes the contagion of reddish leprosy," which is "leprosy flowering in the baldness or in the forehead-baldness." […]

13:12.t: But the second kind of leprosy is, if "it shall have flowered," it says, "in the skin, so that it covers all the skin of the body from the head even to the feet, throughout all things whatsoever the priest shall have inspected." When, then, it shall have covered over "all the skin of the body," then the priest pronounces him to be "clean" from the contagion. But "on whatsoever day there shall appear in him living color," again "he is judged unclean" through this, that "living color has appeared in him" which he did not have before. Concerning this some even before me have said that "living color" indicates the reason of life which is in man; and while this reason is not yet set in the soul, if any of that sin be done, it is not reckoned, for the reason that he who transgresses seems not yet capable of reason; but when reason has found place and time in him, if he now does anything against reason, he is rightly seen to be culpable. […]

13:18.t: The third law concerning lepers is, "when in the skin of the body an ulcer is formed, and in the place of the ulcer a white scar with redness is found." But the cause of an ulcer is when in the body a filthy and noxious humor abounds. So then also in the soul are understood as ulcers those things which boil up from unclean desires or filthy thoughts. And if perchance these have been cured through the grace of faith and the remission of sins, and the soul has been made whole, nevertheless there remains "a scar," and that "scar" does not have a color like that of the body, but is "whiter," it is pronounced to be "leprosy." For a desire is so shining and clear that even to those who look further it shows the indications of the sin residing in it, and perhaps of such a "sin" as is "unto death"; and therefore it is described not only to be "a white scar," but also "reddish." But as to his saying that the scar itself "appears lower," it is certain that a stain of sin of this kind makes the soul lowly and cast down.

13:24.t: The fourth was the law, where it is said that "if in the skin there comes a burning of fire," and after these things, "when the burning has been healed, it itself becomes shining and white with redness, or certainly whitish, and the appearance of it is lower than the rest of the skin": and this he says is "the leprosy which has flowered in the burning." See, then, whether "a burning" is not in every soul whatsoever that receives "the fiery darts of the evil one"; or whether everyone who burns in carnal love is not "scorched by fire." These, then, are the "burnings" and kindlings of "fire." But also he suffers "a burning" who is set ablaze by desire of human glory, and who is inflamed by the heats of anger or fury. […]

We read in Leviticus, if indeed we read with open eyes, and the veil that is placed upon the law does not shut out the gaze of the inner eye, that leprosy is wont to arise in the weal and scar of a burn, and to change the color of the hair, and that a new foulness is added to the former disfigurement of the scar. This is so for this reason: that no one, secure about repentance because after sin he can say: I will endure the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my cause, should sin and need cautery, and, once healed, be wounded again.

13:29.t: The fifth kind of leprosy is when "a contagion is formed on the head or in the beard of a man or a woman, so that the appearance of the contagion itself is lower than the skin of the body; and this is the leprosy of the head or of the beard." See, then, whether it can happen that "leprosy of the head" be thought to be in him who has not "Christ as his head," but some other — for example, Epicurus, who preaches pleasure as the highest good; does not both the head and the beard of such a man seem to you unclean? But also he who, whereas he ought to be a man and to act as one perfect, if perchance he is easily and as a boy overcome by sin, he too must be said to have "leprosy of the beard," because, whereas he ought to overcome the evil one and to proceed with priestly honor, which is designated in the beard, hindered by the vices of adolescence, he suffers "leprosy of the beard." […]

13:40.t: Now the sixth and last kind of leprosy is set down, which "comes in baldness or forehead-baldness"; which things, as far as they are in themselves, are clean. For thus also the law says: "If any one's," it says, "hairs of the head have fallen off, he is bald, he is clean. But if they have fallen off from his forehead, he is forehead-bald, he is clean." And these things are suitably referred to the soul, so that, when it casts off and lays aside those things which are dead by their own nature, it is said to be clean. But after this, if those things which had first been purified shall be seen to sprout up again, filthier and lower than the dignity of purity requires, they will render the soul unclean and leprous.

13:45.t: From this now, generally, concerning every leper in whom there shall have been "the contagion of leprosy" and it shall appear "lower than the rest of the skin" — for every vice of the soul is lower than its remaining virtues — the law, which "is spiritual," decrees certain such things: "Let his garments," it says, "be unstitched, and his head uncovered, and his mouth covered over." By which it designates that he who is leprous in soul, that is, who is fixed fast with sins, ought not to sew coverings upon himself and to cover over the baseness of sin. For just as he whose "garments are unstitched" bears the baseness of his body naked and uncovered, so ought he who is hedged about with some sins to cover his evils and disgraceful deeds with no sewn-on words, with no veils of excuses; so that he may not become "a whited sepulchre, which outwardly indeed appears beautiful to men, but within is full of the bones of the dead and of all uncleanness." […]

13:46.t: "He shall be unclean," it says, "and shall sit separated outside, his dwelling shall be outside the camp." It is clear that every "unclean" one is cast out from the assembly of the good and separated from the company and camps of the saints; and therefore it says that: "his dwelling shall be outside the camp."

14:2.t: But if perchance he shall have been made clean, he does not indeed come of his own accord and by himself to the priest, but is offered, it says, by another, nor does he enter into the camp. For neither was it fitting that "on the same day on which he was made clean," before those things which were suitable were done for him, "he should enter into the camp." On account of which "the priest," it says, "shall go out to him outside the camp." For always to him who cannot yet "enter into the camp" there "goes out" that one who can "go out outside the camp," who says: "I went out from God and came into this world." "The priest goes out," then, "to him" and considers whether he now receives health, whether he is being purged from the contagion of leprosy.

And whoever will may see the profound and mighty mystery of Christ written for our benefit in Leviticus. For the law of Moses declares the leper defiled, and gives orders for him to be put out of the camp as unclean: but should the malady ever be alleviated, it commands that he should then be capable of readmission. Moreover it clearly specifies the manner in which he is to be pronounced clean, thus saying; "This is the law of the leper on whatsoever day he shall have been cleansed, and shall be brought unto the priest. And the priest shall go out of the camp, and the priest shall see him, and behold, the touch of the leprosy is healed from the leper: and the high priest shall command, and they shall take for him who is cleansed two living clean birds; […]
14:2.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

14:4.t: But when the priest shall have seen him, he commands that "there be taken two living hens for him who is being made clean, and cedar wood and twisted scarlet and hyssop." It seems to me that here too these "two hens" have a certain likeness of the two goats, of which one is offered to the Lord and the other is sent forth "into the wilderness"; for so here also, of the two hens, one is immolated and the other is let go "into the field." He, then, who is being purged of leprosy gives here too some part which is cast away "into the wilderness"; but the other part is offered to the Lord for him. Yet not yet does this one, who is being purged of leprosy and offers the hens, offer at the altar even that very hen which is offered for him to the Lord, as "turtledoves or doves." For not yet "on the same day" is he who is being purged of leprosy made worthy of the divine altar. On account of which the lawgiver commands that "on the same day on which he is purged, two hens be taken" for his purification. […]

Take for me a Jew reading Leviticus, and all those sacraments that are written there, and how the leper enters into the synagogue, how a hen is taken up, and its neck is wrung; then it is told how the blood is to be sprinkled, it is told of the water, it is told also of the hyssop, it is told too how his garments are to be rent, and thus he enters into the synagogue, he who had been a leper. If we read according to the letter, what profit is it to us that we read? But if we have turned to the heart, if we have understood spiritually, we shall see that the leper cannot enter to the people of God unless his garments be rent, unless whatever had been shut up be uncovered. Then see that this leper does not enter into the synagogue except through blood and water and hyssop. Therefore you too, who up to this day have been a leper — your leprosy did not appear until you came to the priest. […]

The Lord also commanded Moses that if any leper were cleansed, he should come to the priest and offer two sparrows to the priest. Of these the priest, sacrificing one, should let its blood run down into living waters; and dipping the living sparrow into the waters into which he had made the blood of the sacrificed sparrow run down, together with cedar wood, scarlet wool, and hyssop, he should sprinkle the leper seven times, and then he would be duly cleansed (Lev. 14:1–7). By the priest Christ is understood; and by the two sparrows the teachers of the two Testaments are understood. By the living waters, moreover, the teachings of the Gospel are indicated, of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (Jn. 7:38). He calls them living waters because they grant eternal life to those who do them. […]

14:5.t: Yet observe also this, that the priest himself is not said to immolate the hen; for not yet is this one, who was a leper, worthy that the priest himself immolate for him. On account of which neither is the blood of the hen offered at the altar, but it says that "the hen shall be slain in an earthen vessel, in which vessel living water has been put," so that both water may be taken up for purification and the fullness of the mystery be completed in "water and blood," which is said "to have gone out from the side" of the Savior, and no less in what John sets down in his epistle and says, that purification is made "in water and blood and spirit." Whence here too I see all these things fulfilled. For there is the "spirit" of that hen which is slain, and the "living water" which is in the vessel, and the "blood" which is poured out over it; […]

14:6.t: See, then, how both the "living hen and the cedar wood and the twisted scarlet and the hyssop are dipped in the blood of the young bird and in living water," so that from this, sprinkled and purified from the "water and blood" in which that "hen" too was dipped which is sent forth "into the field," and sprinkled "seven times toward the Lord," he who is being purified may be made clean from all the uncleanness by which he had been possessed from the contagion of leprosy.

14:8.t: But note also this, how, whereas above he had said: "This is the law of the leper; on the day on which he shall have been made clean," now he adds to all these things and says: "and he shall be clean." For if the leprosy having once been cast off he "has been made clean," how shall he still "be clean"? But see that, even if anyone be made clean from sin and be no longer in the act of sin, nevertheless the very traces of the crime committed need purification, both that which we have expounded and, no less, others which are commanded in what follows. For we have observed that to this — that it is written concerning leprosy: "on the day on which he shall have been made clean" — after these things, among the other things which are commanded, it is said a third time: "and he shall be clean," and again at the last it is written: "and he shall be cleansed." Whence it seems to me that there are certain differences even in the purification itself, and, so to say, certain advances of the purgations. […]

14:9.t: Yet he is not immediately permitted to enter his own house, but it is said that he "remain outside his own house for seven days, and shave every hair of his head and beard and eyebrows"; as though it had not been enough that he had first "shaved every hair," now it is added that he "shave every hair of his head and beard and eyebrows." For the same thing seemed to have been said in that he had said "every hair was to be shaved." But this repetition does not seem to me to be empty. For he wills, after the sinner shall have been made clean, after he shall have received through repentance the remission of sins, to admonish him concerning the purgation "of the head and of the beard and of the eyebrows," as if he were saying to him: "Behold, thou art now made whole," see that thou contract no further guilt of the head. For "the sin of the head" is to think otherwise concerning the divine doctrines than the faith of the Church holds. […]

14:10.t: "And the offering of fine flour, sirs," I said, "which was prescribed to be presented on behalf of those purified from leprosy, was a type of the bread of the Eucharist, the celebration of which our Lord Jesus Christ prescribed, in remembrance of the suffering which He endured on behalf of those who are purified in soul from all iniquity, in order that we may at the same time thank God for having created the world, with all things therein, for the sake of man, and for delivering us from the evil in which we were, and for utterly overthrowing principalities and powers by Him who suffered according to His will.

But these things happen when he is indeed set within the camp, yet still "outside his own house." For it says after seven days: "on the eighth day he shall take to himself two lambs." Now not another "takes," but he himself "takes to himself." "Two lambs," it says, "without blemish, and one yearling ewe without blemish, and three tenths of fine flour sprinkled with oil, and one cyathus of oil," so that after these things, purified by a fifth purification, he may be brought to completion. Of these "two lambs," then, one indeed is immolated and is said to be "for the trespass": "in the place," it says, "in which he is slain for sin, and where the whole burnt offerings are made, in the holy place." Behold, now he is made worthy to offer sacrifice, who was able to arrive at the fifth purification, and his victim becomes "the holy of holies." But the other lamb is made "a whole burnt offering," in which also "the priest is said to make propitiation for him, that he may be purged." […]

14:14.t: And after, according to those things which were said above, the victims are offered for purification, he applies, it says, also "the cyathus of oil" and separates it "before the Lord." "And the priest," it says, "shall take of the blood, and shall put it upon the tip of his right ear and upon the extremity of his right hand and upon the extremity of his right foot." And after these things, it says, "the priest shall take" not the cyathus of oil itself, but "of" it, and "shall pour it out," it says, "into his own left hand, and the priest shall dip his finger in the oil which is in his left hand, and shall sprinkle it seven times before the Lord"; and again: "of that which remains in his left hand, he shall put it upon the right ear of him who is being purified, and upon the extremity of his right hand and upon the extremity of his right foot"; and after these things: "that which shall have been left of the oil, the priest shall put," it says, "from his hand upon the head of him who is being purified." […]

16:1.t: The Day of Atonement is needed by all who have sinned, and therefore among the solemnities of the law, which contain the figures of the heavenly mysteries, there is held a certain solemnity which is called the Day of Atonement. This, then, which has now been read out, is the legislation of that very solemnity which, as we have said, is called the Day of Atonement. But let us see first what the content of the letter itself intends, so that, while you pray — provided that you so beseech the Lord that you may deserve to be heard — we may be able to receive the grace of the Spirit, through which we may have strength to explain the mysteries which are contained in the law. "Two sons of Aaron died, Nadab and Abihu, when they offered strange fire at the altar of the Lord." […]

16:4.t: But first of all let us show how these things which are written concerning the sacrifices the Apostle says are "figures" and "forms", whose truth is shown in other things, lest perchance the hearers should think that we presume and violently bend the law of God to another sense than that in which it is written — that is, if no Apostolic authority in these things which we assert should go before. Paul therefore, writing to the Hebrews, namely to those who indeed read the law and had these things meditated upon and well known, but had need of understanding as to how one ought to think concerning the sacrifices, says in this manner: "for Jesus entered not into the holy place made with hands, the copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, that he might now appear before the face of God for us." And again he says of the victims: "for this he did once, by offering himself as a victim." But why do we seek testimonies concerning these things one by one? […]

16:7.t: The mystery of the passion may be seen also in another instance. For according to the Mosaic law two goats were offered, differing in nothing from one another, but alike in size and appearance. Of these, one was called "the lord:" and the other, the "sent-away." And when the lot had been cast for that which was called "lord," it was sacrificed: while the other was sent away from the sacrifice: and therefore had the name of the "sent-away." And Who was signified by this? The Word, though He was God, was in our likeness, and took the form of us sinners, as far as the nature of the flesh was concerned. The goat, then, male or female, was sacrificed for sins. But the death was our desert, inasmuch as by sin we had fallen under the divine curse. But when the Saviour of all Himself, so to speak, undertook the charge, He transferred to Himself what was our due, and laid down His life, that we might be sent away from death and destruction.
16:7.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

16:8.t: May I offer, moreover, an interpretation of the two goats which were presented on "the great day of atonement"? Do they not also prefigure the two natures of Christ? They were of like size and very similar in appearance, owing to the Lord's identity of aspect. He is not to come in any other form. He had to be recognized by those by whom he was also wounded and pierced. One of these goats was bound with scarlet and driven by the people out of the camp into the wilderness, amid cursing, and spitting, and pulling and piercing, being thus marked with all the signs of the Lord's own passion. The other, by being offered up for sins and given to the priests of the temple for meat, afforded proofs of his second appearance, when (after all sins have been expiated) the priests of the spiritual temple, that is, the church, are to enjoy the flesh, as it were, of the Lord's own grace. The rest will deport from salvation without tasting it.

Now indeed concerning the victims, some are commanded to be the high priest's own, but others are "to be taken from the people". His own is said to be the "bull-calf", which among animals is more precious and stronger; and the second animal, the "ram", which among sheep is without doubt more precious. But from the people the gifts are commanded to be offered: a "ram" from the leaders and "two goats" from the people; one that is to be sent away "into the wilderness", which is also named "the scapegoat", and one that is to be offered to the Lord. If the whole people of God were holy and all were blessed, there would not be made two lots over the goats, and one indeed bear the lot to be sent away "into the wilderness", but the other to be offered "to the Lord", but there would be one lot and one victim to the Lord alone. […]

But that which we say concerning the lot, let not the hearer take it as though some such lot is meant as is wont to be conducted among men by chance and not by judgment. "The Lord's lot" is to be taken as though one should say the choice of the Lord or the portion of the Lord, and again the lot of that one which is sent "into the wilderness" is to be taken as that portion which, for its own unworthiness, is spurned and cast off by the Lord. For indeed the very word "scapegoat" contains the signification of one cast off and rejected. From which we can also understand this, for example: an evil thought ascends into your heart, a desire of another man's wife or of a neighbor's possession; understand at once that this is of "the lot of the scapegoat", cast it off immediately and expel it from your heart. How do you cast it off? […]

Yet since the word of God is rich and, according to the judgment of Solomon, is to be "inscribed upon the heart" not simply, but doubly and "triply," let us try even now to add some things to those which were spoken a while ago according to our strength, that we may show how, "in a type of things to come," here too one goat was offered to the Lord as a victim and the other was sent away "alive." Hear in the Gospels Pilate saying to the priests and the people of the Jews: "Which of the two do you wish that I release to you, Jesus who is called Christ, or Barabbas?" Then all the people cried out that he should release "Barabbas," but hand Jesus over to death. Behold, you have the goat which was sent away "alive into the wilderness," bearing with itself the sins of the people that cried out and said: "Crucify, crucify!" […]

16:12.t: Let us see after these things what the things are which the high priest does: "and he shall take" it says "a censer full of coals of fire from the altar which is before the Lord". We read also in Isaiah that the prophet is purged by fire through "one of the seraphim, which was sent to him, when it took with tongs one coal from those which were upon the altar, and touched the lips of the prophet and said": "behold, I have taken away your iniquities". To me these things seem to be mystical and to indicate this, that to each one, according to that in which he sins, if he is worthy to be purified, coals are applied to his members. For since the prophet here says: "I have unclean lips, and I dwell also in the midst of a people having unclean lips", therefore the "coal taken up with the tongs" by the seraph purges his lips, in which alone he professes himself not to be clean. From which it is shown that only as far as the word was his sin found, but that in deed or work he had sinned in nothing; […]

"And he shall take" it says "a censer full of coals". Not all are purged by that fire which is taken "from the altar". Aaron is purged by that fire, and Isaiah, and any who are like them; but others, who are not such, among whom I reckon even myself, we shall be purged by another fire — I fear lest by that of which it is written: "a river of fire ran before him". That "fire" is not "from the altar". The fire which is "from the altar" is the fire of the Lord; but that which is outside the altar is not the Lord's, but is the proper fire of each one of those who sin, of which it is said: "their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished". That "fire" therefore is of those very ones who kindled it, as also elsewhere it is written: "walk in your fire and in the flame which you have kindled for yourselves". […]

Therefore the high priest "takes a censer full of coals of fire from the altar which is before the Lord, and fills his hand with the fine incense of composition and carries it into the interior of the veil". Let us understand first what the history designates, and then let us inquire what the spiritual sense holds. Twofold is the house of the tabernacle of testimony or of the temple of the Lord. The first is that in which is the "altar of the whole burnt offerings", which is stirred up with perpetual fires, in which house it is lawful for the priests alone to stand and to celebrate the rites and ministries of the sacrifices, and to neither the Levites nor anyone else besides is access granted. But the second house is the interior one, separated from this only by a "veil". Within which veil are the "ark of the testament" and the "propitiatory", upon which the "two cherubim" are set, and the "altar of incense" is placed. […]

16:13.t: The divine word therefore says: "and he shall place incense upon the fire in the sight of the Lord, and the smoke of the incense shall cover the propitiatory which is over the testimonies, and he shall not die. And he shall take of the blood of the bull-calf and shall sprinkle with his finger upon the propitiatory toward the east". The rite indeed of atonement for men among the ancients, which was made to God, he has taught how it should be celebrated; but you, who have come to Christ, the true high priest, who by his blood made God propitious to you and reconciled you to the Father, do not cling to the blood of the flesh; but learn rather the blood of the Word, and hear him saying to you: "this is my blood, which shall be poured out for you for the remission of sins". He who is imbued with the mysteries knows both the flesh and the blood of the Word of God. Let us not therefore linger in these things which are both known to those who know and cannot lie open to those who are ignorant. […]

16:17.t: After these things the Scripture adds: "and there shall not be" it says "a man, when the high priest enters within the interior veil in the tabernacle of testimony". How "shall there not be a man"? I understand it thus, that he who has been able to follow Christ and to penetrate with him the interior tabernacle and to ascend the heights of the heavens, shall now "not be a man", but according to his own word shall be "as an angel of God". Or perhaps even that word will be fulfilled concerning him which the Lord himself said: "I said, you are gods and sons of the Most High, all of you". Whether therefore, made spiritual, he becomes one spirit with the Lord, or through the glory of the resurrection passes into the order of angels, rightly he will now "not be a man"; but each one himself provides this for himself, that he either exceed the appellation of man or be reckoned within the condition of this word. […]

16:21.t: But let us see who this is who receives that one whose "lot has become the scapegoat's", that he may cast him "into the wilderness". "A man" it says "ready shall receive the goat which has come into his lot, upon whom the lot of the scapegoat has fallen, and shall lead him away into the wilderness." The end of this lot is the "wilderness", that is, a deserted place, deserted of virtues, deserted of God, deserted of righteousness, deserted of Christ, deserted of every good. And so upon each of us too awaits one lot of the two. For either, acting well, we are "the Lord's lot", or, acting badly, our lot leads us "to the wilderness". Do you wish that I show you evidently how those two lots are always at work and each one of us becomes either "the Lord's lot" or "the scapegoat's" or "the wilderness'"? […]

What follows, To be ready, is to be read in two ways: either so that "to be ready for every good work" is understood; or else, joining what he says, to obey for every good work, with what precedes and ending it there, to be ready is, as it were, another precept of its own and a special one, in keeping with what is written in Leviticus: "The goat that is sent away, bearing the curses of the people, is to be handed over into the hands of a ready man" (Lev. 16:21). If, then, anyone is ready to hold the ἀποπομπαῖον (the scapegoat), and lead it out into the desert, and there destroy it, and, so far as in him lies, banish it by the lot of the curse, he, when he has obeyed, will also be ready for every good work.

And that which is said in a sacred manner in Leviticus, where in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, Aaron offers for the people the scapegoat, and that a living one, and, laying his hands upon its head, calls down upon it all the sins of the people of Israel, and hands it over into the hands of a prepared man, and sends it into the desert, this we understand of ourselves, and, preparing ourselves at the command of the true priest, we remove evil from the midst of the Church.

In another place also it is written that the Lord commanded Moses that the sons of Israel should offer to the priest the scapegoat, and that the priest should lay his hands on its head and confess over it the sins of the sons of Israel and send it by a man who was ready into the wilderness, so that it might carry the sins of the sons of Israel into the wilderness. But the one who led the scapegoat into the wilderness was not allowed to enter the camp unless he first washed his garments (Lev. 16:21-26). Therefore the priest has the same meaning as the scapegoat; for they signify our Lord Jesus Christ. So the priest confessed over the scapegoat the sins of the sons of Israel, because the Son of God placed the sins of humanity upon the man whom he assumed, so that he himself would die for them. By the wilderness, whose dwelling all lovers of luxury dread, the cross is signified, very terrible to all who are guilty. […]

16:26.t: Perhaps in another way also "the man ready" and clean, who "leads away that one whose lot has come, into the wilderness", and by that very act by which he leads him out, as one who has touched something unclean, is said to "wash his garments" at evening and to be clean — perhaps even our Lord and Savior himself may be understood, in that part in which he took on the "garments" of our nature, that is, of flesh and blood, which he "washed at evening"; on account of which also the prophet had long ago said of him: "and I saw Jesus the great priest, clothed in filthy garments, and the devil standing at his right hand, that he might contradict him." Therefore he "washed his robe in wine" — that is, in his own blood — "at evening", and was made "clean". And thence perhaps it was that after the resurrection he said to Mary, who wished to hold his feet: "do not touch me." But do you wish to see yet another form of the two lots? […]

16:29.t: We indeed, who are of the Church, rightly receive Moses and read his writings, understanding this about him: that he is a prophet, and that, by God's revealing to him, he wrote down in symbols and figures and allegorical forms the mysteries to come, which we teach to have been fulfilled in their own time. But whoever does not receive in him a meaning of this kind, whether he be one of the Jews or even one of our own, cannot show him to be a prophet at all; for how will he prove him a prophet, whose letters he asserts to be commonplace, aware of nothing future and containing no hidden mystery? And so, as this man who thinks in this way reads these things, the divine word rebukes him and says: "Do you suppose you understand what you read?" There is, then, the law, and all the things that are in the law, according to the Apostle's judgment, "imposed until the time of correction"; […]

Ours, therefore — that is, we who do not "serve the shadow and the copy," but the truth — this is the Day of Atonement for us, on which the remission of sins has been given to us, when "Christ our Passover has been sacrificed." How then, having come to know the truth, "do we turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements of this world, to which you wish to be enslaved anew from the beginning, observing days and months and seasons and years?" Hear how the prophet too rejects a fast of this kind and says: "This is not the fast I have chosen, says the Lord, nor a day for a man to humble his soul." You, if you wish to fast according to Christ and "to humble your soul," every time of the whole year lies open to you; nay rather, have all the days of your whole life "for humbling your soul," if indeed you "have learned" from the Lord our Savior "that he is meek and humble of heart." When, then, is there for you no day of humiliation, you who follow Christ, who is "humble of heart" and the master of humility? […]

17:11.t: The troubling utterance is the following: "The soul of all flesh is the blood" — behold an extremely difficult passage, which has shaken those who did not understand it! … According to my measure of understanding, and with prayer for help in the knowledge of the Divine utterances … I have observed that incorporeal things are given the same names as corporeal things, and thus corporeal things are related to the outer man, while those bearing the same names as the corporeal are related to the inner man. Scripture says that in man there are two. … Therefore in each of us there are two men. Why does the Holy Scripture say that the soul of all flesh is the blood? This is a difficult question. Just as the outer man is homonymous with the inner one, so also with respect to the parts of the body. One may say that each part of the body of the outer man is homonymous with the corresponding part of the inner man. … And so, everything that is in the sentient flesh you can find also in the inner man. […]

And this thought, I hold, was not due to accident, nor was its source in man, but it was divinely suggested. For when they saw since they were holy, brought nigh to God, and enlightened by the Divine Spirit in their souls that there was need of great stress on the cleansing of the sons of men, they thought that a ransom was due to the source of life and soul in return for their own salvation. And then as they had nothing better or more valuable than their own life to sacrifice, in place of it they brought a sacrifice through that of the unreasoning beasts, providing a life instead of their own life. They did not consider this was sinful or unrighteous. They had not been taught that the soul of the brutes was like man's, which has discourse of reason: they had only learned that it was the animal's blood, and that in the blood is the principle of life, which they offered themselves, sacrificing as it were to God one life instead of another. […]
17:11.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 1, Chapter 10

17:11.t: For the flesh of the Savior is for the salvation of the body, but the blood was poured out for our soul, just as had been prefigured earlier by Moses; for so he says: The flesh is offered for your body, but the blood for the soul (Lev. 17:11); and therefore blood is not to be eaten.

18:3.t: It is written, he says, in Leviticus “Neither shalt thou take a wife to her sister, to vex her, to uncover her nakedness, beside the other in her life time.” From this it is plain, he argues, that it is lawful to take her when the wife is dead. To this my first answer shall be, that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law; otherwise we shall be subject to circumcision, the sabbath, abstinence from meats. For we certainly must not, when we find anything which falls in with our pleasures, subject ourselves to the yoke of slavery to the law; and then, if anything in the law seems hard, have recourse to the freedom which is in Christ. We have been asked if it is written that one may be taken to wife after her sister. Let us say what is safe and true, that it is not written. But to deduce by sequence of argument what is passed over in silence is the part of a legislator, not of one who quotes the articles of the law. […]

18:4.t: Conjugal chastity accords with the written law by reason of the divine statute, Leviticus 18. For the Lord established laws according to which legitimacy is observed in the persons who contract marriage. For He says: I am the Lord your God: keep my laws and judgments, which if a man do, he shall live in them. No man shall approach to her that is near of kin to him, etc. Since therefore the Lord as a benefit promised that He would give offspring to Abraham through the way of marriage, and miraculously made fruitful the dead womb of Sarah, and also gave laws according to which marriage is to be contracted: it is evident that conjugal chastity accords with the written law.
18:4.s: Disputed Questions on Evangelical Perfection, Question 3

18:5.t: The righteousness of the law is proposed in these terms,-that whosoever shall do it shall live in it; and the purpose is, that when each has discovered his own weakness, he may not by his own strength, nor by the letter of the law (which cannot be done), but by faith, conciliating the Justifier, attain, and do, and live in it. For the work in which he who does it shall live, is not done except by one who is justified. His justification, however, is obtained by faith; and concerning faith it is written, "Say not in thine heart, Who shall ascend into heaven? (that is, to bring down Christ therefrom;) or, Who shall descend into the deep? (that is, to bring up Christ again from the dead.) But what saith it? The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart: that is (says he), the word of faith which we preach: That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised Him from the dead, thou shalt be saved." As far as he is saved, so far is he righteous.
18:5.s: ON THE SPIRIT AND THE LETTER 29.50

18:5.t: Wherefore we ought to know that we from whom the requirements of the law are no longer exacted, but in whose ears the word of the gospel daily sounds: "If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell all that thou hast and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven, and come follow Me," when we offer to God tithes of our substance, are still in a way ground down beneath the burden of the law, and not able to rise to those heights of the gospel, those who conform to which are recompensed not only by blessings in this present life, but also by future rewards. For the law promises to those who obey it no rewards of the kingdom of heaven, but only solaces in this life, saying: "The man that doeth these things shall live in them." But the Lord says to His disciples: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven;" […]
18:5.s: The First Conference of Abbot Theonas, Chapter 5

18:6.t: I, however, maintain that this point has not been left in silence, but that the lawgiver has made a distinct prohibition. The words “None of you shall approach to any one that is near of kin to him, to uncover their nakedness,” embraces also this form of kinsmanship, for what could be more akin to a man than his own wife, or rather than his own flesh? “For they are no more twain but one flesh.” So, through the wife, the sister is made akin to the husband. For as he shall not take his wife’s mother, nor yet his wife’s daughter, because he may not take his own mother nor his own daughter, so he may not take his wife’s sister, because he may not take his own sister. And, on the other hand, it will not be lawful for the wife to be joined with the husband’s kin, for the rights of relationship hold good on both sides.

18:18.t: It is written, he says, in Leviticus “Neither shalt thou take a wife to her sister, to vex her, to uncover her nakedness, beside the other in her life time.” From this it is plain, he argues, that it is lawful to take her when the wife is dead. To this my first answer shall be, that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law; otherwise we shall be subject to circumcision, the sabbath, abstinence from meats. For we certainly must not, when we find anything which falls in with our pleasures, subject ourselves to the yoke of slavery to the law; and then, if anything in the law seems hard, have recourse to the freedom which is in Christ. We have been asked if it is written that one may be taken to wife after her sister. Let us say what is safe and true, that it is not written. But to deduce by sequence of argument what is passed over in silence is the part of a legislator, not of one who quotes the articles of the law. […]

19:2.t: Recently there was recited in the ears of the Church the word of God saying: "Be holy, for I too am holy, the Lord your God". What this name "holy" intends for itself, and what it signifies in the divine Scriptures, must be inquired into more diligently, so that, when we have learned the force of the word, we may also be able to fulfill its work. Let us therefore gather from the divine Scriptures those things over which we find the word "holy" said, and we discover that not only human beings, but even dumb animals are called "holy"; we find also that "vessels" of the ministry are called "holy", and that vestments are said to be "holy", and no less the places which are set within cities or suburbs and assigned to the priests. Among the dumb animals indeed, the "firstborn" of oxen or of flocks are commanded by the law to be sanctified to the Lord, and it is said: do not, it says, perform any work with them, since they are sanctified to the Lord. […]

To be sanctified is to be drawn away from any love that sullies and corrupts and may lead the soul to ruin. In this must the creature resemble the Creator: "You shall be holy," He said, "because I am holy." This holiness makes one God-conformed. That is why the Seraphic spirits cried out: "Holy, holy, holy."

19:9.t: During the harvest, [the law] forbids owners to gather up the bits which fall from the sheaves and similarly advises that in harvesting something should be left behind unreaped. By this it gives excellent teaching to owners in the practice of generous sharing by leaving some of their property for those in need and providing the poor with a chance for food.

Do you see how the law proclaims simultaneously the justice and goodness of God, who provides food unstintingly for all? Again, in the grape harvest the harvesters are forbidden to go back and cut anything that has been left over or to collect fallen grapes. The same rules are applied to olive gatherers. In fact the principle of tithing crops and flocks was an education in honoring the divine. We are not to be totally absorbed by profit but to share humanely with the neighbor as well.

19:14.t: For to curse the deaf is to disparage one who is absent and does not hear; but to put a stumbling-block before the blind is to act indeed with discernment, but yet to give cause of offence to him who has not the light of discernment.
19:14.s: THE BOOK OF PASTORAL RULE, Part 3

19:15.t: "You shall not be partial to the poor," a precept given lest under pretext of showing pity we should judge an unjust judgment. For each individual is to be judged not by his personal importance but by the merits of his case. His wealth need not stand in the way of the rich man, if he makes a good use of it; and poverty of itself can be no recommendation to the poor if in the midst of squalor and want he fails to stay away from wrongdoing.

19:17.t: But why should we spend any more time over evangelic and apostolic precepts, when even the old law, which is thought to be some- what slack, guards against the same thing, when it says, "Thou shall not hate thy brother in thine heart;" and again, "Be not mindful of the injury of thy citizens;" and again, "The ways of those who preserve the recollection of wrongs are towards death"? You see there too that wickedness is restrained not only in action, but also in the secret thoughts, since it is commanded that hatred be utterly rooted out from the heart, and not merely retaliation for, but the very recollection of, a wrong done.
19:17.s: The Twelve Books on the Institutes of the Coenobia, Book 8, Chapter 15

19:18.t: The second commandment is like it, since it is the love of a human being who was made according to the image of God, and perhaps also according to his likeness. But in the exposition of the commandment which is set down concerning the love of one's neighbor, these things also must be said. For, according to what is said in the tenth Psalm, "he who loves iniquity hates his own soul", and according to what is said in Proverbs, "he who rejects discipline hates himself", it is manifest that no one who loves iniquity loves his neighbor as himself, since he does not even love himself; and no one who rejects discipline loves his neighbor as himself, seeing that he does not love his very self either. And thus it comes about that he who "loves iniquity", and "hates his own soul", cannot keep the second commandment. Likewise also "he who rejects discipline" loves some sin; and therefore he too who rejects any word of God's discipline "hates his own soul".

Let him use those tenths and first-fruits, which are given according to the command of God, as a man of God; as also let him dispense in a right manner the free-will offerings which are brought in on account of the poor, to the orphans, the widows, the afflicted, and strangers in distress, as having that God for the examiner of his accounts who has committed the disposition to him. Distribute to all those in want with righteousness, and yourselves use the things which belong to the Lord, but do not abuse them; eating of them, but not eating them all up by yourselves: communicate with those that are in want, and thereby show yourselves unblameable before God. For if you shall consume them by yourselves, you will be reproached by God, who says to such unsatiable people, who alone devour all, "You eat up the milk, and clothe yourselves with the wool;" [Ezekiel 34:3] and in another passage, "Must you alone live upon the earth"? […]

For since it is written in the law: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself," he is proven to love his neighbor less who does not share with him even those things necessary to himself in his neighbor's time of need. Therefore the precept is given about dividing two tunics with one's neighbor, because this could not be said of one tunic, since if one is divided, no one is clothed. For with half a tunic, both he who receives remains naked and he who gave remains naked.

19:36.t: And the giver of the law similarly forbids the same thing, saying: "Let the balance be just and the weights equal, the bushel just and the sextarius equal," and Solomon also gives a like opinion on this matter: "Great and small weights and double measures are both unclean before the Lord, and one who uses them shall be hindered in his contrivances." Further not only in the way in which we have said, but also in this must we strive not to have unfair weights in our hearts, nor double measures in the storehouse of our conscience, i.e., not to overwhelm those, to whom we are to preach the word of the Lord, with precepts that are too strict and heavier than we ourselves can bear, while we take for granted that for ourselves those things which have to do with the rule of strictness are to be softened by a freer allowance of relaxation. For when we do this, what is it but to weigh and measure the goods and fruits of the Lord's commands in a double weight and measure? […]
19:36.s: The First Conference of Abbot Theonas, Chapter 22

20:8.t: After these things it is written: "keep", it says, "my precepts and do them, I am the Lord", and to these it added: "a man, a man, if he shall have cursed his father or his mother, let him die"; and after many things which it commanded, to which it also appended the penalties of transgression, it adds in the conclusion: "and keep all my precepts and my justifications and my judgments". Whence it seems to me consequent to inquire what is indicated in these single terms. For my part, according to what I have been able to observe, a "precept" or "commandment" is that which, for example, in the decalogue is said: "you shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery"; for this only is enjoined, and the penalty of the deed is not appended. But now indeed the same things are repeated, but with penalties added; for it is said: "a man, a man, whoever shall have committed adultery with the wife of a man and the wife of his neighbor, by death let him die, he who commits adultery and she who is committed adultery with. […]

20:9.t: But when we wish to examine the very letter of the words as given by Matthew, "He that speaks evil of father or mother, let him die the death," consider whether it was taken from the place where it was written, "Whoso strikes his father or mother, let him die the death; and he that speaks evil of father or mother, let him die the death." For such are the exact words taken from the law with regard to the two commandments; but Matthew has quoted them in part and in an abridged form, and not in the very words.
20:9.s: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 11.9

20:9.t: Among the other sins therefore which are punished with death, the divine law reports that also "he who shall have cursed his father or mother, by death let him die". The name of father is a great mystery, and the name of mother is a hidden reverence. Your father according to the spirit is God; your mother is the "heavenly Jerusalem". Learn these things from prophetic and apostolic testimonies. This same Moses writes in the canticle: "is not this same one your father who acquired you and possessed you?". But the Apostle says concerning the "heavenly Jerusalem" that: "she is free", he says, "who is the mother of us all". First, therefore, your father is God, who begot your spirit, who also says: "I have begotten sons and exalted them". But James the Apostle also says: "let us obey the father of spirits and we shall live". Secondly, your father is the father of the flesh, by whose ministry you were born in the flesh and came into this world, who carried you "in his loins"; […]

20:10.t:
A woman accused of adultery was brought by the Scribes and Pharisees to the Lord Jesus with the malicious intent, that, if He was to acquit her, He might seem to annul the Law, if He condemned her, that He might seem to have changed the purpose of His coming, since He came to remit the sins of all men. To the same purport He said above, "I judge no man." So when they brought her they said, "This woman was taken in adultery, in the very act; now Moses in the Law commanded us that such should be stoned, but what sayest Thou?"

While they were saying this, Jesus stooped down and wrote with His finger on the ground. And as they waited for His answer, He lifted up His head and said, "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her." What can be more Divine than this sentence, that he should punish sins who is himself free from sin? For how can we endure one who takes vengeance on guilt in another and excuses it in himself? […]

21:10.t: Everyone who is a priest among men is small and slight in comparison with that priest of whom God said: "you are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek". But he is the "great priest" who is able "to penetrate the heavens" and to pass beyond the whole of creation and to ascend to him who "dwells in light inaccessible", the God and Father of the universe. For this reason the one too who among the Jews was called the "great priest" did indeed enter into the holy places, but ones made by hand, built of stones; he did not ascend into heaven nor was he able to stand before the "Father of lights". But because he was fulfilling the shadow and image of these things, therefore also he bore the name of "great priest" by way of shadow and image. […]

"And the great priest" it says "from among his brethren, upon whose head the oil of anointing has been poured and who has his hands perfected to put on the holy vestments, shall not take the mitre from his head, shall not rend his garments, and shall not go in to any dead soul; in his father or in his mother he shall not be defiled, and he shall not go out from the holy places and shall not pollute the name which is hallowed, the name of God upon him, because the holy oil of the anointing of his God is upon him; I am the Lord. He shall take to wife a virgin of his own kindred. But a widow and one cast out and one defiled and a harlot, these he shall not take; but he shall take to wife a virgin of his own kindred; and he shall not defile his seed among his people; I am the Lord, who sanctify him". Among the Jews too there was indeed an image of this observance, and the things which the law appointed were kept by the high priests of the Jews; […]

But after these things: "upon whom" it says "the oil of anointing has been poured, upon his head". Do not seek on earth that "oil" which is poured "upon the head" of the "great priest" that he may become Christ; but if it seems good, learn from the prophet David what this "oil" is: "you have loved" he says "righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows". This, then, is the "oil of gladness" which, "poured upon his head", made him Christ. But it adds still further to his praises: "who has his hands perfected" it says. To what man, I ask, is it fitting that this be said? In what mortal can we find "perfect hands"? Even if this be Aaron, of whom mention seems to be made, how will he be thought to have had "perfected hands", with which "he fashioned the calf", with which he carved an idol? Even if you bring forward Moses himself, how will he seem to have had "perfected hands", who did not glorify the Lord "at the water of contradiction"? […]

21:11.t: "And he shall not go in to any dead soul". What is a "dead soul"? One that is dead; the prophet says: "the soul that sins, it shall die". Upon this dead soul, then, Christ does not come, because he is "wisdom", and wisdom does not enter into a malevolent soul. For that soul is dead, because in whom malice is present, sin also is present. "And sin, when it is consummated" it says "begets death". And on account of this Jesus "does not enter in to a dead soul". But if the soul lives, that is, if it has not in itself a mortal sin, then Christ, who is "life", comes to the living soul; because just as "light cannot be with darkness nor righteousness with iniquity", so neither can life be with death. And therefore if anyone is conscious to himself that he has within him a mortal sin and has not cast it from himself through the repentance of fullest satisfaction, let him not hope that Christ "enters in to" his "soul", who "does not enter in to any dead soul", because he is the "great priest".

"In his father and in his mother he shall not be defiled". This passage of Scripture is most difficult to explain, but if by your prayers you entreat God the Father of the Word to deign to enlighten us, by his own gift it will be able to be explained. Everyone who enters this world is said to be brought into being in a certain defilement. On account of which Scripture also says: "no one is clean from filth, not even if his life be of one day". This very thing, then — that he is placed "in the womb" of his mother and that he takes the material of his body from the origin of the paternal seed — can be said to be "defiled in father and mother". Or do you not know that, when a male child has been made forty days old, he is offered at the altar, that he may there be purified, as one who was polluted in the very conception, whether of the paternal seed or of the maternal womb? […]

21:12.t: But our Lord Jesus Christ alone, "who knows no sin", "was defiled neither in father nor in mother" and "did not go out from the holy places". There were indeed some things to be set before the Jews in the passages above, to which they could not respond, but omitting those, what do they for the present tell us on this discourse, either they themselves or those who wish the law to be understood according to their sense: if these things are not referred to our high priest and Savior, how will it be proved according to the letter that "the great priest did not go out from the holy places", who nevertheless even took a wife, as is said below, "a virgin of his own kindred"? If "he does not go out from the holy places", if he goes forth nowhere, how or for what uses is he commanded to "take a wife"? For it must not be supposed that he could remain within the holy places with a wife. But let those suppose these things to whom "Jewish fables" are pleasing. […]

But He is said to have been brought up at Nazara, and also to have been called a Nazarene We know that the Hebrew word "Naziraion" occurs in Leviticus in connection with the ointment which they used for unction. And the ruler there was a kind of image of the great and true High Priest, the Christ of God, being a shadowy type of Christ. So there it is said about the High Priest according to the Septuagint: "And he shall not defile him that is sanctified to his God, because the holy oil of his God hath anointed him": where the Hebrew has nazer for oil. And Aquila reads: "Because the separation, the oil of God's unction, is on him"; and Symmachus: "Because the pure oil of his God's anointing is on him ": and Theodotion: "Because the oil nazer anointed by his God is upon him." So that nazer according to the Septuagint is "holy," according to Aquila "separation," according to Symmachus "pure," and the name Nazarene will therefore mean either holy, or separate, or pure. […]
21:12.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 7, Chapter 2

21:12.t: And so your soul will be carried forward not only to the ark of the Divine Covenant, but also to the priestly kingdom, and owing to its unbroken love of purity being as it were engrossed in spiritual studies, will fulfil the command given to the priests, enjoined as follows by the giver of the Law: "And he shall not go forth from the sanctuary, lest he pollute the Sanctuary of God," i.e., his heart, in which the Lord promised that he would ever dwell, saying: "I will dwell in them and will walk among them."
21:12.s: The First Conference of Abbot Nesteros, Chapter 10

21:13.t: But what is added after these things? "He shall take to wife a virgin of his own kindred, but a widow and one cast out and a harlot he shall not take, but he shall take a virgin of his own kindred; and he shall not defile his seed among his people; I am the Lord, who sanctify him". Since therefore the order of the whole exposition has been recalled to the true "great priest", Christ, let us now see also what ought to be understood about his nuptials. Paul the Apostle says: "but I wish to present you all as a chaste virgin to one husband, to Christ. But I fear lest, as the serpent seduced Eve by his craftiness, your senses be corrupted from the simplicity which is in Christ". Paul therefore wishes to "present all the Corinthians as a chaste virgin to Christ"; which assuredly he would never wish, unless he saw it to be possible. Whence perhaps it may seem wonderful how these, who came to the faith of Christ corrupted by diverse sins, are all together called a "chaste virgin"; […]

"But a widow and one cast out and one defiled he shall not take". If any of us has sinned, he is "cast out"; even if he is not cast out by the bishop, whether because it lies hidden or because he is sometimes judged unto grace, he is nevertheless "cast out" by the very consciousness of sin. Nor does the grace of man avail, when Christ does not receive such a soul into marriage as "cast out". Therefore "neither a widow", as we said above, "will he take, nor one cast out nor one polluted". She is called "polluted" who, even if she has not completely committed the sin, yet by this very thing that she thought it, that she wished it, that she desired it, even if she did not carry it out, is "polluted" and is not chosen by the "great high priest". For he requires an exceedingly pure, exceedingly clean and sincere soul, which he may join to himself, because "he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit". […]

21:14.t: But also "a harlot he shall not take". What is a "harlot" soul? One that receives to itself "lovers", of whom the prophet says: "you have played the harlot after your lovers". Who are these "lovers" who enter in to the harlot soul, except the adverse powers and demons, who conceive desire of her beauty? For the soul was created beautiful by God and exceedingly comely. Hear how God himself says: "let us make man according to our image and likeness". See of what comeliness, of what beauty the soul is; it has the "image and likeness" of God. When the adverse powers behold this beauty, that is, "the devil and his angels", they covet its form; and because they cannot become its bridegrooms, they desire to play the harlot with it. If therefore you receive, O man, into the bedchamber of your soul the adulterer "devil", your soul has played the harlot with the devil. If you receive "his angels", if diverse spirits that persuade you to sin, your soul has played the harlot with them; […]

21:17.t: I know also that not even bodily blemishes in either priests or victims passed without notice, but that it was required by the law that perfect sacrifices must be offered by perfect men—a symbol, I take it, of integrity of soul.

21:20.t: Hence also it is said through Moses that whoever is burdened with a hump should by no means be advanced to the priesthood. And all of us who have been redeemed by the blood of Christ are made members of that same high priest. Whence also it is said to us through Peter: "But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood." But he who bears a hump always gazes at the lowest things. Therefore he is driven from the priesthood, because whoever is intent only on earthly things is himself a witness to himself that he is not a member of the high priest.

22:14.t: At the end, it is stated, "If a man eats of the sanctified things through ignorance, iniquity and wickedness are laid at his feet, and he shall be bound by a vow." Thus also the apostle teaches us that we are to eat the Eucharist of the Lord with caution, lest we eat to our condemnation and judgment. If ignorance is condemned under the law, how much more will full knowledge be condemned according to the gospel?

22:20.t: Since then it is impossible to be saved, unless we do those works which are according to the commandment of God, nor is it without danger to neglect any precept—for it is terrible arrogance to make ourselves the judges of our Lawgiver, and to approve some of His laws and reject others—let us who endure the conflict of piety and lead the life of calm and rest, regard such a life with honour, as being our fellow worker in keeping the Gospel decrees, and one and all take careful heed that no commandment escape us. For if the man of God must be perfect—as it is written, and as our words have already shown—it is before all things necessary that he be made perfect in every commandment, according to “the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ”; for by the divine law a beast with a blemish, even if he was clean, was not accepted as a sacrifice to God.

22:27.t: Scripture says, "At least grant the offspring to its mother for its first seven days." For if nothing comes to be without reason and milk flows in the mothers for the nourishment of the offspring, then in taking the offspring away from the providential endowment of the milk, a person is doing violence to nature. So Greeks and anyone else who runs the law down ought to blush for shame if the law is generous over irrational beasts. Yet some people actually expose human offspring to abortive death. By prophetic authority the law has for a long time cut short their ferocity through this commandment of which we have been speaking. For if the law refuses to allow the offspring of irrational creatures to be separated from their mother before taking milk, it is far more forceful in preparing human beings against that cruel, uncivilized view [exposure to death of infants]. If they ignore nature, at least they may not ignore the lessons of the law.

23:8.t: He it was rather who kept it, who was without sin. For this is the spiritual Sabbath, to have no sin. In fact, brethren, it is of this that God admonishes us, when He commends the Sabbath to our notice: "Thou shalt do no servile work" These are God's words when commending the Sabbath, "Thou shalt do no servile work." Now ask the former lessons, what is meant by servile work; and listen to the Lord: "Every one that committeth sin is the servant of sin." But these men, neither seeing, as I said, nor anointed, kept the Sabbath carnally, and profaned it spiritually.

23:15.t:
Germanus: Why then do we relax the rigour of our abstinence in our meals all through the fifty days, whereas Christ only remained with His disciples for forty days after His resurrection?

Your pertinent question deserves to be told the perfect true reason. After the Ascension of our Saviour which took place on the fortieth day after His Resurrection, the apostles returned from the Mount of Olives, on which He had suffered them to see Him when He was returning to the Father, as the book of the Acts of the Apostles also testifies, and entered Jerusalem and are said to have waited ten days for the coming of the Holy Ghost, and when these were fulfilled on the fiftieth day they received Him with joy. […]
23:15.s: The First Conference of Abbot Theonas, Chapters 19-20

23:17.t: Two loaves of bread made from the first fruits of the new harvest were rightly ordered to be offered, for the church gathers those it can consecrate to its Redeemer as a new family from both peoples, the Jews and the Gentiles.

23:27.t:
That we may be able to shew what kind of persons we should be when we fast, and of what character the fast should be, listen again to God commanding Moses, and saying, as it is written in Leviticus, ‘And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying, In the tenth day of this seventh month, there shall be a day of atonement; a convocation, and a holy day shall it be to you; and ye shall humble your souls, and offer whole burnt-offerings unto the Lord.’ And afterwards, that the law might be defined on this point, He proceeds to say; ‘Every soul that shall not humble itself, shall be cut off from the people.’

Behold, my brethren, how much a fast can do, and in what manner the law commands us to fast. It is required that not only with the body should we fast, but with the soul. Now the soul is humbled when it does not follow wicked opinions, but feeds on becoming virtues. For virtues and vices are the food of the soul, and it can eat either of these two meats, and incline to either of the two, according to its own will. […]

23:40.t: He who dwells in tabernacles of this kind, and hastens to go from the tabernacles to the courts, and from the courts to the house, and from the house to the temple of the Lord, ought to celebrate the solemnity of tabernacles with the most beautiful wood of wisdom, of which it is said in Proverbs: It is a tree of life to all who draw near to it, and to those who lean upon it, as upon the Lord of firmness. And with the branches of palms, in which the sign of victory and the reward of virtue are contained; and with the boughs of the thickest tree, which the Jews understand as the myrtle, because of the mortification of vices and lusts. Hence myrrh too is offered as a gift to the Lord and Savior by the magi. And with the branches, he says, of the willow and of the poplar, which some call one tree; and the very name of the wood, which in Greek is called ἀγνὸς, indicates chastity. […]

23:44.t: He who is "perfect" is taught by God himself concerning the meaning of the festivals, and he does not need a man as his teacher for learning these things, but he learns from God, if anyone is able to grasp the voice of God. But he who is not such a one, but of lower rank, learns from him who has learned from God. There is, then, this twofold manner of teaching concerning the festivals. There is the one by which the prophetic mind, illumined through the Spirit, is taught — which, so to speak, is learned more by the gaze of the mind than by the sound of a voice, through which the truth itself, and not the shadow and image of the truth, is recognized. But those who cannot grasp the very brightness of God, nor behold the whole radiance of the truth with the fixed keenness of the mind, hear about the festivals in second place from those who learned first; and while the very property of direct inspection gave to those the truth of things, to these only hearing conveys the shadow of the truth. […]

24:2.t: First, concerning the "lamp" and the "lampstand" and the "oil" which is poured into it; second, concerning the "table" and the "shewbread" and their number and those who ought to use them. Let us therefore direct our mind more diligently to the things that are written, and let us pray that the grace of the Lord be granted us for discerning these things, so that in the letters which we read we may recognize what is the will of the Holy Spirit. "Command", it says, "the children of Israel, and let them bring you clean oil pressed from olives for the light, that a lamp may burn always outside the veil in the tabernacle of testimony, and Aaron and his sons shall kindle it from evening until morning before the Lord without ceasing, an everlasting statute throughout your generations. On the clean lampstand you shall kindle the lamps before the Lord until morning". He names a "clean lampstand"; […]

But "since the law is spiritual", let us ask of the Lord — if indeed "we have turned to the Lord" — that "the veil of the reading of the old testament be taken away" from us, so that we may be able to perceive what is the meaning of his "lampstand and lamps" according to the spiritual understanding. Before the coming of my Lord Jesus Christ the sun did not rise upon the people of Israel, but it made use of "the light of a lamp". For among them the word of the law and the prophetic word was a "lamp" shut within narrow walls, which could not pour out its light upon the whole earth. For within Judea the knowledge of God was confined, as the prophet also says: "God is known in Judea". But when the "sun of righteousness", our Lord and Savior, rose, and the man was born of whom it is written: "behold a man, the East is his name", throughout the whole world the light of the knowledge of God was poured out. […]

24:5.t: But now let us see what is written also in what follows concerning the shewbread. "And you shall take", it says, "fine flour and make from it twelve loaves; of two tenths shall be one loaf; and you shall set them in two rows, six loaves in one row, upon the clean table before the Lord. And you shall put upon the row clean frankincense and salt, and the loaves shall be set as a memorial before the Lord; on the day of the sabbaths they shall always be set forth before the Lord by the children of Israel, an everlasting covenant. And it shall be Aaron's and his sons', and they shall eat them in a holy place; for they are the holy of holies. This shall be theirs of the things that are offered to the Lord, an everlasting statute". According to what is written, in the twelve loaves a "memorial before the Lord" seems to be made of the twelve tribes of Israel, and a command to be given that without ceasing these "twelve loaves be set forth in the sight of the Lord"; […]

But let us now see what is the making of these shewbread loaves which are commanded to be "always placed before the Lord". "Of two tenths", it says, "let there be one loaf". He said "two tenths" indeed, but of what measure these "tenths" are he did not specify; although surely it would have been consistent, if he wished the quantity of the fine flour to be known, to name the measure itself of which he commanded "two tenths" to be taken. What, then, is this thing whose measure and amount could neither be specified nor named? The number ten is everywhere found to be perfect; for from it arises the reckoning and origin of every number. Fittingly, therefore, the author and origin of all things, God, is seen to be shown under this number. But if in the church I speak of the Father alone and utter the praises of him alone, I have made a loaf of one tenth. Or if I make a discourse concerning Christ alone and recount his passion and preach his resurrection, I have offered a "loaf" of one tenth. […]

The Old Covenant had its loaves of proposition, but they, as belonging to that covenant, have come to an end. The New Covenant has its heavenly bread and cup of salvation to sanctify both body and soul. For as the bread is for the body, the Word suits the soul.

The law indeed pointed them out before in type, and the prophets also proclaimed them. As, for instance, it is written in the Mosaic record, "And ye shall take fine flour, and make it into twelve loaves: and he shall put them in two rows upon the pure table before the Lord. And ye shall put upon the row frankincense and salt: and they shall be for loaves, sot before the Lord for a memorial." For the bread that came down from heaven, and giveth life to the world, Who else can it be but Christ the Saviour of the universe? And in imitation too of Him, the blessed disciples also are named loaves: for having been made partakers of Him Who nourishes us unto life eternal, they also nourish by their own writings those who hunger and thirst after righteousness. And as the Saviour Who is the true light called the disciples also light:—"for ye are the light of the world:"—so also being Himself the broad of life, He has bestowed upon His disciples to be ranked as loaves." […]
24:5.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

24:5.t: The twelve loaves on the table of the tabernacle then are the twelve apostles and all those in the church who follow their teaching. Since until the end of time they do not cease to renew the people of God with the nourishment of the word, they are the twelve loaves of proposition which never depart from the table of the Lord. And those same loaves are properly ordered to be made not from just any flour but from the finest wheat, doubtless because all those who minister the word of life to others must first devote themselves to the fruits of virtue. [Thus] they may commend by their actions those things that they counsel in their preaching, being conformed to the example of him who says concerning himself, "Unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone." Those same loaves are also properly commanded to be set on the table in two rows of six for the sake of concord (that is to say, charity and fellowship), for the Lord is also said to have sent his disciples out to preach two by two. […]
